advisory.title: Integer overflow in `BytesMut::reserve`
crossbeam-channel: double free on Drop
advisory.description:
The internal `Channel` type's `Drop` method has a race
which could, in some circumstances, lead to a double-free.
This could result in memory corruption.

Quoting from the
[upstream description in merge request \#1187](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/crossbeam/pull/1187#issue-2980761131):

> The problem lies in the fact that `dicard_all_messages` contained two paths that could lead to `head.block` being read but only one of them would swap the value. This meant that `dicard_all_messages` could end up observing a non-null block pointer (and therefore attempting to free it) without setting `head.block` to null. This would then lead to `Channel::drop` making a second attempt at dropping the same pointer.

The bug was introduced while fixing a memory leak, in
upstream [MR \#1084](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/crossbeam/pull/1084),
first published in 0.5.12.

The fix is in
upstream [MR \#1187](https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/crossbeam/pull/1187)
and has been published in 0.5.15

advisory.title: Invalid pointer dereference in `fmt::Pointer` impl for `Atomic` and `Shared` when the underlying pointer is invalid
advisory.description: Affected versions of `fmt::Display` dereference the underlying pointer. This causes a invalid pointer dereference e.g., when a pointer created with `Atomic::null` or `Shared::null`. `fmt::Debug` impls and pre-0.9 `fmt::Display` impls, which do not dereference pointers, are not affected by this issue.

advisory.title: h2 unbounded empty DATA frames
advisory.description:
The h2 crate, used internally by hyper, had a flaw that would accept and queue empty DATA frames without limit.
If streams were not actively drained, this could lead to unbounded memory usage, or a panic if the length overflows.

Low severity.

Patched in v0.4.16.

advisory.title: h2 unbounded empty DATA frames
advisory.description:
The h2 crate, used internally by hyper, had a flaw that would accept and queue empty DATA frames without limit.
If streams were not actively drained, this could lead to unbounded memory usage, or a panic if the length overflows.

Low severity.

Patched in v0.4.16.

advisory.title: Borsh serialization of HashMap is non-canonical
advisory.description:
The borsh serialization of the HashMap did not follow the borsh specification.
It potentially produced non-canonical encodings dependent on insertion order.
It also did not perform canonicty checks on decoding.

This can result in consensus splits and cause equivalent objects to be
considered distinct.

This was patched in 0.15.1.

advisory.title: `idna` accepts Punycode labels that do not produce any non-ASCII when decoded
advisory.description:
`idna` 0.5.0 and earlier accepts Punycode labels that do not produce any non-ASCII output, which means that either ASCII labels or the empty root label can be masked such that they appear unequal without IDNA processing or when processed with a different implementation and equal when processed with `idna` 0.5.0 or earlier.

Concretely, `example.org` and `xn--example-.org` become equal after processing by `idna` 0.5.0 or earlier. Also, `example.org.xn--` and `example.org.` become equal after processing by `idna` 0.5.0 or earlier.

In applications using `idna` (but not in `idna` itself) this may be able to lead to privilege escalation when host name comparison is part of a privilege check and the behavior is combined with a client that resolves domains with such labels instead of treating them as errors that preclude DNS resolution / URL fetching and with the attacker managing to introduce a DNS entry (and TLS certificate) for an `xn--`-masked name that turns into the name of the target when processed by `idna` 0.5.0 or earlier.

## Remedy

Upgrade to `idna` 1.0.3 or later, if depending on `idna` directly, or to `url` 2.5.4 or later, if depending on `idna` via `url`. (This issue was fixed in `idna` 1.0.0, but versions earlier than 1.0.3 are not recommended for other reasons.)

When upgrading, please take a moment to read about [alternative Unicode back ends for `idna`](https://docs.rs/crate/idna_adapter/latest).

If you are using Rust earlier than 1.81 in combination with SQLx 0.8.2 or earlier, please also read an [issue](https://github.com/servo/rust-url/issues/992) about combining them with `url` 2.5.4 and `idna` 1.0.3.

## Additional information

This issue resulted from `idna` 0.5.0 and earlier implementing the UTS 46 specification literally on this point and the specification having this bug. The specification bug has been fixed in [revision 33 of UTS 46](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr46/tr46-33.html#Modifications).

## Acknowledgements

Thanks to kageshiron for recognizing the security implications of this behavior.

advisory.title: libz-sys build script leaks environment variables in the build directory
advisory.description:
The build script of `libz-sys` version <= 1.1.30 prints the full environment
of the build, including any secrets it contains, to its stdout when compiled
with `cc@1.6.0` or later on a Unix host. This affects any build that depends on
`libz-sys`. Cargo saves build script stdout under `target/`, so the values end
up in anything that stores or shares the `target/` directory, such as CI caches.

This is similar to the [Miri issue](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/09/21/github-actions-leaking-secrets-when-miri-output-is-cached/).

## Details

To decide whether to link against a system zlib, the `libz-sys` build script
compiles a small test program with a compiler command from `cc` and logs it
with:

```rust
println!("running {:?}", cmd);
```

On Unix, `Debug` impl for `std::process::Command` prints every environment
variable explicitly set on the command. Before `cc@1.6.0`, its
`Tool::to_command()` set only a few compiler-specific variables. Starting with
`cc@1.6.0` (released 2026-10-03), `Tool::to_command()` clears the environment
and sets every variable explicitly.

Cargo parses build script stdout for `cargo:` directives, and stores the full
output in the build directory. It also prints it with `-vv`.

The probe runs for a default `libz-sys` build, including when pkg-config finds
zlib, unless one of these applies:

* the target is Windows, Android, Haiku or OpenHarmony
* static linking is requested via the `static` feature or `LIBZ_SYS_STATIC=1`
* the `zlib-ng` features are enabled without `stock-zlib`

## Mitigations

Fixed in `libz-sys@1.1.31`, which no longer logs the probe command.

If you cannot upgrade, here are some workarounds:

* Build with `LIBZ_SYS_STATIC=1` or the `static` feature, which skips the probe.
* Pin `cc` to a release before 1.6.0 (`cargo update cc --precise <version>`).

Note that upgrading `libz-sys` does not remove values already written. If an
affected build already ran with secrets in its environment, clear CI caches and
stored artifacts containing its
[target/build directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/cargo/reference/build-cache.html#build-cache),
and consider rotating those secrets.

advisory.title: Unbounded growth of pending connection ID retirements in quinn-proto
advisory.description:
When processing a NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame, quinn-proto queues a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame for
each connection ID that the peer asked it to retire. The normal path bounds this queue and closes
the connection with a CONNECTION_ID_LIMIT_ERROR if the bound would be exceeded. However, the path
handling a connection ID that had already been retired pushed onto the queue without applying
the limit and without deduplicating.

A peer that has completed the handshake can first send a NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame with a large
`retire_prior_to` value to advance the receiver's connection ID window, and then repeatedly send
NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames with sequence numbers below that window. Each such frame adds another
entry to the queue. The queue is only drained by sending RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames, which are
subject to congestion control, so a peer that withholds acknowledgements can stall the drain while
continuing to flood, growing the victim's memory use without bound.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.17 by applying the same limit on the already-retired path.

Thanks to [@scadastrangelove](https://github.com/scadastrangelove) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Denial of service in Quinn endpoints
advisory.description:
Receiving QUIC transport parameters containing invalid values could lead to a panic.

Unfortunately the maintainers did not properly assess usage of `unwrap()` calls in the
transport parameters parsing code, and we did not have sufficient fuzzing coverage to find this
issue. We have since added a fuzzing target to cover this code path.

advisory.title: Peer minimum ACK delay can panic quinn-proto when ACK_FREQUENCY transmission is enabled
advisory.description:
When sending ACK_FREQUENCY frames is enabled through
`TransportConfig::ack_frequency_config(Some(..))`, the peer's transport parameters could cause
`AckFrequencyState::candidate_max_ack_delay` to call `Duration::clamp` with a minimum greater
than its maximum, which panics.

For example, a peer advertising a `min_ack_delay` of 100,000 microseconds and a `max_ack_delay`
of 100 milliseconds passes transport parameter validation. At a 5 ms RTT, the lower bound of the
clamp becomes 100 ms while the upper bound is 25 ms, violating the precondition of `clamp` and
panicking while driving the connection. Both automatically derived and explicitly configured
maximum ACK delays use this calculation.

Sending ACK_FREQUENCY frames is disabled by default, so only endpoints that opt in are affected.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.18 by computing the delay with explicit minimum and maximum bounds
instead of `clamp`.

Thanks to [@zerox80](https://github.com/zerox80) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Remote memory exhaustion in quinn-proto from unbounded out-of-order stream reassembly
advisory.description:
The `Assembler` component that assembles unordered stream fragments into consecutive chunks of the
stream incurs some overhead for non-contiguous fragments. Readers that read from a RecvStream in
order (through an `AsyncRead` impl for example) will be sensitive to peers that send fragments
while leaving out early parts of the stream, and in particular, fragments with many gaps (because
these cannot be defragmented). In such a scenario, the receiving connection suffers from high
buffer overhead, enabling memory exhaustion.

advisory.title: Zero-length DATAGRAM frames bypass the receive buffer limit in quinn-proto
advisory.description:
quinn-proto bounds its queue of received datagrams by charging each queued frame's payload length
against `TransportConfig::datagram_receive_buffer_size`, evicting the oldest datagrams when the
limit is exceeded. A DATAGRAM frame with an empty payload was charged zero bytes, so it never
triggered eviction and was appended to the queue, which has no other bound.

DATAGRAM frames are not subject to flow control. A peer that has completed the handshake can
therefore send a stream of empty DATAGRAM frames and grow the receiver's heap without limit until
the process is killed. An application that reads incoming datagrams but does so more slowly than
the peer sends them is still affected. Receiving datagrams is enabled by default, so all endpoints
that do not explicitly set `datagram_receive_buffer_size(None)` are affected.

The send path had the same accounting flaw: an application could enqueue an unbounded number of
empty outgoing datagrams without ever receiving `SendDatagramError::Blocked`.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.17 by accounting for the fixed per-datagram overhead in both
directions, so that every queued datagram consumes buffer space.

Thanks to [@alexpyattaev](https://github.com/alexpyattaev) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Remote peer can panic quinn-proto with zero-length STREAM frames during unordered reads
advisory.description:
When a stream is read in unordered mode (for example through `RecvStream::read(false)` in
quinn-proto or `read_unordered` in `quinn`), quinn-proto proactively deduplicates received data
by recording received ranges in a `RangeSet` through its `replace` method. When an incoming
STREAM frame carried an empty payload, the `Drop` implementation of the iterator returned by
`replace` inserted an empty range into the set, violating the invariant that stored ranges are
non-empty. Subsequent frames overlapping that region then caused a panic while processing the
stream.

A remote peer can trigger this with five small STREAM frames (two of them zero-length) once the
application has put the stream in unordered-read mode. The default ordered read path is not
affected.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.18 by ignoring empty ranges in `RangeSet::replace`.

Thanks to Otto Hermann ([@ojhermann](https://github.com/ojhermann)) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Some AES functions may panic when overflow checking is enabled.
advisory.description:
`ring::aead::quic::HeaderProtectionKey::new_mask()` may panic when overflow
checking is enabled. In the QUIC protocol, an attacker can induce this panic by
sending a specially-crafted packet. Even unintentionally it is likely to occur
in 1 out of every 2**32 packets sent and/or received.

On 64-bit targets operations using `ring::aead::{AES_128_GCM, AES_256_GCM}` may
panic when overflow checking is enabled, when encrypting/decrypting approximately
68,719,476,700 bytes (about 64 gigabytes) of data in a single chunk. Protocols
like TLS and SSH are not affected by this because those protocols break large
amounts of data into small chunks. Similarly, most applications will not
attempt to encrypt/decrypt 64GB of data in one chunk.

Overflow checking is not enabled in release mode by default, but
`RUSTFLAGS="-C overflow-checks"` or `overflow-checks = true` in the Cargo.toml
profile can override this. Overflow checking is usually enabled by default in
debug mode.

advisory.title: Unauthenticated ServerHello can downgrade later connections to classical key exchange
advisory.description:
The client recorded the server-selected key exchange group for each server
name when processing the ServerHello, before the server was authenticated.
This record is used to predict which key share to send in future ClientHellos
to that server name.

A network attacker can answer one connection attempt with a ServerHello
selecting X25519, and then close the connection. Later ClientHellos for that
name carry only an X25519 key share, while `supported_groups` still lists
X25519MLKEM768 first. If the genuine server accepts that share rather than
sending a HelloRetryRequest for its preferred hybrid group, the handshake
completes with classical-only key exchange and no error. This persists for as
long as the entry stays in the client's session store.

The impact is loss of post-quantum confidentiality for affected connections
("harvest now, decrypt later"). There is no key compromise and no
authentication bypass.

The following are not affected:

- connections to servers which send a HelloRetryRequest for their preferred group,
- clients with resumption disabled (as nothing is stored), and
- other server names.

This behaviour is discussed in
[draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction-01.html#name-security-considerations),
so the practical impact depends largely on server policy.

advisory.title: TLS 1.3 handshake messages incorrectly accepted across encryption level boundaries
advisory.description:
Rustls accepted TLS 1.3 handshake messages sent at the wrong encryption level
when they followed a key-changing message in the same record. For example,
a plaintext `EncryptedExtensions` message packed into the same record as the
`ServerHello` was accepted.

RFC 8446 section 5.1 requires that handshake messages do not span key changes,
and that implementations terminate the connection with an "unexpected_message"
alert if they do.

The handshake transcript is still authenticated, so a network-position attacker
cannot use this to alter or complete a handshake; the practical effect is that
a peer could send handshake messages that should be encrypted in plaintext
without rustls rejecting the connection.

This is functionally the same bug as Go's
[GO-2026-4340](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-4340) (CVE-2025-61730).

advisory.title: Brotli certificate decompression can allocate up to 1 GiB before authentication
advisory.description:
The built-in Brotli certificate decompressor (enabled by the non-default
`brotli` crate feature) bounded the size of the decompressed output, but
accepted a peer-selected history window. Brotli's large-window extension was
enabled, so a five-byte header could cause an allocation of 1 GiB. A peer can
abort a process whose allocator cannot satisfy that request.

No trusted certificate is required by the attacker. Affected configurations are:

- clients that enable the `brotli` feature and connect to a malicious server, and
- servers that enable the `brotli` feature and request client certificates.

Applications that do not enable the `brotli` feature are not affected.

advisory.title: `Debug` impls for client session values expose TLS secrets
advisory.description:
The `Debug` implementations of `Tls12ClientSessionValue` and
`Tls13ClientSessionValue` were derived, and so included the TLS 1.2 master
secret or TLS 1.3 resumption PSK in their output.

Custom `ClientSessionStore` implementations that format these values with
`Debug` (for example, when logging) could disclose these secrets to readers of
the logs. This conflicts with rustls's
[key-material redaction policy](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/99f2358cae2954837dbb866faf6727de75489ab9/SECURITY.md#boundary-public-api).

Ordinary connection and built-in session cache `Debug` output is redacted and
is not affected.

advisory.title: rustls network-reachable panic in `Acceptor::accept`
advisory.description:
A bug introduced in rustls 0.23.13 leads to a panic if the received
TLS ClientHello is fragmented.  Only servers that use
`rustls::server::Acceptor::accept()` are affected.

Servers that use `tokio-rustls`'s `LazyConfigAcceptor` API are affected.

Servers that use `tokio-rustls`'s `TlsAcceptor` API are not affected.

Servers that use `rustls-ffi`'s `rustls_acceptor_accept` API are affected.

advisory.title: Certificate verification may accept distrusted intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys when the configured trust anchors allow such paths.
The private keys corresponding to these intermediates are now well known.

Versions 0.103.16 and 0.104.0-alpha.8 reject paths containing these public keys.

advisory.title: Reachable panic in certificate revocation list parsing
advisory.description:
A panic was reachable when parsing certificate revocation lists via [`BorrowedCertRevocationList::from_der`]
or [`OwnedCertRevocationList::from_der`].  This was the result of mishandling a syntactically valid empty
`BIT STRING` appearing in the `onlySomeReasons` element of a `IssuingDistributionPoint` CRL extension.

This panic is reachable prior to a CRL's signature being verified.

Applications that do not use CRLs are not affected.

Thank you to [@tynus3](https://github.com/tynus3) for the report.

advisory.title: CRLs not considered authoritative by Distribution Point due to faulty matching logic
advisory.description:
If a certificate had more than one `distributionPoint`, then only the first `distributionPoint` would be considered against each CRL's `IssuingDistributionPoint` `distributionPoint`, and then the certificate's subsequent `distributionPoint`s would be ignored.

The impact was that correctly provided CRLs would not be consulted to check revocation. With `UnknownStatusPolicy::Deny` (the default) this would lead to incorrect but safe `Error::UnknownRevocationStatus`. With `UnknownStatusPolicy::Allow` this would lead to inappropriate acceptance of revoked certificates.

This vulnerability is thought to be of limited impact. This is because both the certificate and CRL are signed -- an attacker would need to compromise a trusted issuing authority to trigger this bug.  An attacker with such capabilities could likely bypass revocation checking through other more impactful means (such as publishing a valid, empty CRL.)

More likely, this bug would be latent in normal use, and an attacker could leverage faulty revocation checking to continue using a revoked credential.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-pwjx-qhcg-rvj4](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-pwjx-qhcg-rvj4). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: Name constraints for URI names were incorrectly accepted
advisory.description:
Name constraints for URI names were ignored and therefore accepted.

Note this library does not provide an API for asserting URI names, and URI name constraints are otherwise not implemented.  URI name constraints are now rejected unconditionally.

Since name constraints are restrictions on otherwise properly-issued certificates, this bug is reachable only after signature verification and requires misissuance to exploit.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: Name constraints were accepted for certificates asserting a wildcard name
advisory.description:
Permitted subtree name constraints for DNS names were accepted for certificates asserting a wildcard name.

This was incorrect because, given a name constraint of `accept.example.com`, `*.example.com` could feasibly allow a name of `reject.example.com` which is outside the constraint.
This is very similar to [CVE-2025-61727](https://go.dev/issue/76442).

Since name constraints are restrictions on otherwise properly-issued certificates, this bug is reachable only after signature verification and requires misissuance to exploit.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-xgp8-3hg3-c2mh](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-xgp8-3hg3-c2mh). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: Denial of Service via Stack Exhaustion
advisory.description:
## Impact

When user-provided input is provided to any type that parses with the RFC 2822 format, a denial of
service attack via stack exhaustion is possible. The attack relies on formally deprecated and
rarely-used features that are part of the RFC 2822 format used in a malicious manner. Ordinary,
non-malicious input will never encounter this scenario.

## Patches

A limit to the depth of recursion was added in v0.3.47. From this version, an error will be returned
rather than exhausting the stack.

## Workarounds

Limiting the length of user input is the simplest way to avoid stack exhaustion, as the amount of
the stack consumed would be at most a factor of the length of the input.

advisory.title: Bundled root certificates allow trust in distrusted emSign intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions include `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, which can allow certificate
paths through distrusted emSign intermediates.

Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys. The private keys corresponding to these intermediates
are now well known.

Version 1.0.10+ removes this root.

The `webpki-roots` 0.26.11 compatibility package contains no independent trust
store and re-exports the roots from its separately resolved 1.x dependency.
That parent dependency must resolve to 1.0.10 or newer; an older parent remains
affected by this advisory.

advisory.title: WebAssembly allocator shim corrupts memory on allocation failure
advisory.description:
On wasm32, zstd-sys provides `malloc` and `free` to the C library through a
shim over Rust's allocator. The shim did not check for allocation failure:
it wrote its size header to address 0 and returned address 4, which the C
library used as a valid buffer. `free(NULL)` also read below address 0.

Whenever the instance cannot grow its memory by what a frame asks for, a
small crafted frame (a 9-byte header declaring a 128 MiB window is enough)
made decompression write decoded data over the bottom of the module's
linear memory, instead of failing. The corruption stays within the wasm
sandbox.

The flaw was corrected by returning NULL on allocation failure or size
overflow, and by making `free(NULL)` a no-op.

advisory.description:

The crate does not seem to have much dependencies and may or may not be ok to use as-is.

advisory.title: `atty` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The maintainer of `atty` has [published](https://github.com/softprops/atty/commit/5bfdbe9e48c6ca6a4909e8d5b04f5e843a257e93) an official notice that the crate is no longer

advisory.title: Bincode is unmaintained
advisory.description:
Due to a doxxing and harassment incident, the bincode team has taken the decision to cease development permanently.

The team considers version 1.3.3 a complete version of bincode that is not in need of any updates.

* [postcard](https://crates.io/crates/postcard)
* [bitcode](https://crates.io/crates/bitcode)

advisory.description:

advisory.title: `pin-utils` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The [upstream repository] was archived on October 1, 2026, after the
release of version 0.1.1.

For local pinning, replace `pin_mut!` with [`core::pin::pin!`], available
since Rust 1.68. For pin projection, replace `unsafe_pinned!` and
`unsafe_unpinned!` with [`pin-project`] or [`pin-project-lite`].

[upstream repository]: https://github.com/rust-lang/pin-utils
[`core::pin::pin!`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/pin/macro.pin.html
[`pin-project`]: https://crates.io/crates/pin-project
[`pin-project-lite`]: https://crates.io/crates/pin-project-lite

advisory.title: proc-macro-error is unmaintained
advisory.description:
proc-macro-error's maintainer seems to be unreachable, with no commits for 2 years, no releases pushed for 4 years, and no activity on the GitLab repo or response to email.

proc-macro-error also depends on `syn 1.x`, which may be bringing duplicate dependencies into dependant build trees.

## Possible Alternative(s)

- [manyhow](https://crates.io/crates/manyhow)
- [proc-macro2-diagnostics](https://github.com/SergioBenitez/proc-macro2-diagnostics)

advisory.title: rustls-pemfile is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The rustls-pemfile crate is no longer maintained. The repository has been archived since August
2025, and users are encouraged to depend directly on the underlying PEM parsing code included
in rustls-pki-types since 1.9.0. The latest version of rustls-pemfile is in fact a thin wrapper
around the same code used in rustls-pki-types, so migrating should be straightforward.

The new API is represented by the [`PemObject`][PemObject] trait, which provides methods for
reading a single or multiple PEM objects from a file or byte slice.

[PemObject]: https://docs.rs/rustls-pki-types/latest/rustls_pki_types/pem/trait.PemObject.html

advisory.title: unsafe-libyaml is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The [repository](https://github.com/dtolnay/unsafe-libyaml) was archived by
its owner on 2024-03-25 and is read-only. The last release is 0.2.11
(March 2024).

`unsafe-libyaml` is a machine translation of libyaml's C code into unsafe
Rust (c2rust). Bugs found in it will not be fixed upstream. It is used by
`serde_yaml` (itself deprecated) and by forks such as `serde_yaml_ng`.

## Alternatives

Consider a YAML parser written in safe Rust, for example:

- [saphyr](https://crates.io/crates/saphyr) ([serde-saphyr](https://crates.io/crates/serde-saphyr) for serde users)
- [noyalib](https://crates.io/crates/noyalib)

advisory.title: Unsoundness in `Error::downcast_mut()`
Potential unaligned read
advisory.description:
On windows, `atty` dereferences a potentially unaligned pointer.

In practice however, the pointer won't be unaligned unless a custom global allocator is used.

In particular, the `System` allocator on windows uses `HeapAlloc`, which guarantees a large enough alignment.

# atty is Unmaintained

A Pull Request with a fix has been provided over a year ago but the maintainer seems to be unreachable.

Last release of `atty` was almost 3 years ago.

## Possible Alternative(s)

The below list has not been vetted in any way and may or may not contain alternatives;

 - [std::io::IsTerminal](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/trait.IsTerminal.html) - Stable since Rust 1.70.0
 - [is-terminal](https://crates.io/crates/is-terminal) - Standalone crate supporting Rust older than 1.70.0

advisory.title: `event-listener` allows `!Send` tags to cross thread boundaries via `StackSlot`
advisory.description:
Affected versions of `event-listener` unconditionally implement `Send` and
`Sync` for `StackSlot<'_, T>`, the stack-allocated listener type created
by the `listener!` macro.

This allows a `!Send` tag type set via `Event::with_tag` to be moved to
another thread and accessed via `StackSlot::wait`, causing a data race in safe
code.

advisory.title: `hex_decode_unchecked` AVX2 path reads past `src`
advisory.description:
`faster_hex::hex_decode_unchecked` is a safe function. On x86 and x86_64, when AVX2 is enabled, `hex_decode_avx2` keeps decoding while `dst.len() >= 32` and then loads 32 bytes from `src` and 32 bytes from `src[32..]`. Nothing in that loop requires `src` to contain 64 bytes.

A safe caller can pass a short `src` and a `dst` of at least 32 bytes. The AVX2 load then reads outside `src`.

The function has had this shape since 0.3.0. 0.10.0 is the last release with the unbounded AVX2 read. The maintainer agreed to this advisory and shipped the backport in 0.10.1 (pull request 74): the AVX2 loop now requires `src.len() >= 64` before those loads. 1.0.0 rewrites `hex_decode_unchecked` so the decoded length is `min(src.len() / 2, dst.len())`. Both are covered by `>= 0.10.1`. Other architectures take the scalar fallback and are outside this advisory.

advisory.title: Unsoundness in opt-in ARMv8 assembly backend for `keccak`
advisory.description:
### Summary

The `asm!` block enabled by the off-by-default `asm` feature, when enabled on ARMv8 targets, misspecified the operand
type for all of its operands, using `in` for pointers and values which were subsequently mutated by operations performed
within the assembly block.

### Impact

It's unclear what practical impact, if any, this actually had. Incorrect operand types are technically undefined
behavior, however changing them had no actual impact on the generated assembly for these targets. The possibility still
exists that it may lead to potential memory safety or other issues on hypothetical future versions of rustc.

### Mitigation

The operand types were changed from `in` to `inout`, and the impacted versions of the `keccak` crate were yanked.

advisory.title: Fails to ensure slice elements match the slice's declared type
advisory.description:
Affected versions allow populating a DistributedSlice of T with elements of an
arbitrary other type that coerces to T. For example, elements of type `&&str`
could end up in a slice of type `[&str]`, since `&&str` coerces to `&str` via a
deref coercion.

The flaw was corrected by implementing typechecking for distributed slice
elements in such a way that coercion no longer occurs. The element's type must
be a subtype of the slice's declared element type.

advisory.title: Potential use-after-free due to lack of panic safety in `LruCache::pop()`
advisory.description:
`LruCache::pop()` in `lru` was not panic-safe. If the `Drop` implementation of a stored key panics during `pop()`, `self.detach()` is never called, leaving dangling pointers in the internal doubly-linked list.

A subsequent cache operation that triggers eviction can then dereference these dangling pointers:
- The node is freed from the map, but remains linked in the LRU list due to the skipped `detach()` call
- When a new insertion causes eviction, the LRU traversal encounters the dangling pointer
- This results in a write to already-freed memory during the eviction process

## Impact

- **CWE-416 (Use-After-Free):** memory corruption when subsequent cache operations access freed node pointers in the linked list
- **CWE-415 (Double Free):** potential heap corruption when the same memory is freed multiple times

Both types of undefined behavior can be invoked in safe Rust, but only if unwinding panics are enabled and `std::panic::catch_unwind` is used with key types that have potentially-panicking `Drop` implementations.

## Fix

Fixed in `lru` 0.18.2 by detaching the node from the linked list before freeing it and dropping the key ([lru-rs#238](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/pull/238)).

advisory.title: `IterMut` violates Stacked Borrows by invalidating internal pointer
advisory.description:
Affected versions of this crate contain a soundness issue in the `IterMut`
iterator implementation. The `IterMut::next` and `IterMut::next_back`
methods temporarily create an exclusive reference to the key when
dereferencing the internal node pointer.

This invalidates the shared pointer held by the internal `HashMap`,
violating Stacked Borrows rules.

advisory.title: Rand is unsound with a custom logger using `rand::rng()`
advisory.description:
It has been reported (by [@lopopolo](https://github.com/lopopolo)) that the `rand` library is [unsound](https://rust-lang.github.io/unsafe-code-guidelines/glossary.html#soundness-of-code--of-a-library) (i.e. that safe code using the public API can cause Undefined Behaviour) when all the following conditions are met:

- The `log` and `thread_rng` features are enabled
- A [custom logger](https://docs.rs/log/latest/log/#implementing-a-logger) is defined
- The custom logger accesses `rand::rng()` (previously `rand::thread_rng()`) and calls any `TryRng` (previously `RngCore`) methods on `ThreadRng`
- The `ThreadRng` (attempts to) reseed while called from the custom logger (this happens every 64 kB of generated data)
- Trace-level logging is enabled or warn-level logging is enabled and the random source (the `getrandom` crate) is unable to provide a new seed

`TryRng` (previously `RngCore`) methods for `ThreadRng` use `unsafe` code to cast `*mut BlockRng<ReseedingCore>` to `&mut BlockRng<ReseedingCore>`. When all the above conditions are met this results in an aliased mutable reference, violating the Stacked Borrows rules. Miri is able to detect this violation in sample code. Since construction of [aliased mutable references is Undefined Behaviour](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/nomicon/references.html), the behaviour of optimized builds is hard to predict.

advisory.title: Broadcast channel calls clone in parallel, but does not require `Sync`
advisory.description:
The broadcast channel internally calls `clone` on the stored value when
receiving it, and only requires `T:Send`. This means that using the broadcast
channel with values that are `Send` but not `Sync` can trigger unsoundness if
the `clone` implementation makes use of the value being `!Sync`.

Thank you to Austin Bonander for finding and reporting this issue.

advisory.title: `AsyncFd::new` and related constructors violate I/O safety
advisory.description:
`tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd` provides safe constructors (`new`, `with_interest`, `try_new`, and `try_with_interest`) that accept any `T: AsRawFd` rather than requiring proof of ownership or validity of the file descriptor. Because `RawFd` implements `AsRawFd`, safe code can construct an `AsyncFd` from an arbitrary or closed file descriptor, or close/replace the underlying file descriptor while the `AsyncFd` is still alive.

This violates I/O safety in two ways:

1. `AsyncFd<T>` implements `AsFd` for all `T: AsRawFd` by calling `BorrowedFd::borrow_raw(self.as_raw_fd())`, allowing safe code to obtain an arbitrary `BorrowedFd<'_>` without owning the file descriptor.
2. Tokio's I/O driver stores a pointer to an internal allocation in the `epoll`/`kqueue` user data for registered file descriptors. If the underlying file descriptor is duplicated and then closed while an `AsyncFd` is alive, and the OS reuses that file descriptor number for a another IO resource on the same runtime, dropping the first `AsyncFd` deregisters the reused file descriptor number and frees the first while the original file description remains registered in `epoll`, leading to a use-after-free when a readiness event fires.

Starting in Tokio 1.51.6, 1.53.3, and 1.54.0, `AsyncFd::new`, `AsyncFd::with_interest`, `AsyncFd::try_new`, and `AsyncFd::try_with_interest` are deprecated in favor of the `unsafe` constructors `AsyncFd::register` and `AsyncFd::register_with_interest`. Callers must ensure that the file descriptor remains valid, open, and unchanged for the lifetime of the `AsyncFd`.
